# [Timeline Columns in Grids](https://neomjs.com/raw/learn/guides/datahandling/Timeline.md)
Source: https://neomjs.com/learn/guides/datahandling/Timeline

---
seoTitle: "Using a Timeline Column in a Grid | Neo.mjs"
seoDescription: "Learn how to add a timeline column to an existing Neo.mjs grid, connect event records to resource rows, configure the time axis, and render interactive timeline bars."
---

# Using a Timeline Column in a Grid

You already have a grid of resources, projects, people, or machines. Now you need to see when work happens alongside the information you already display.

A conventional grid answers *what belongs to each row*. A timeline adds another question: *when does it happen?*

You do not need to replace your grid with a scheduler to answer that question. Neo.mjs provides `Neo.timeline.Column`, a grid column that projects time-based records into horizontal bars inside the corresponding row. Your existing resource columns remain ordinary grid columns; the timeline becomes another column in the same layout.

## 1. What a Timeline Column adds

`Neo.timeline.Column` extends `Neo.grid.column.Base`. It turns a row's time-based data into bars positioned against a shared `Neo.timeline.TimeAxis`.

This is useful when a timeline is one part of a larger tabular view. For example, a project grid can keep its owner, status, and priority columns while adding a schedule next to them. A machine inventory can show machine details and operating intervals in the same row.

The relationship looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Resources["Grid store<br/>Resource rows"]
    Grid["Neo.grid.Container"]
    Events["Neo.timeline.store.Events<br/>Event records"]
    Axis["Neo.timeline.TimeAxis<br/>Date range and scale"]
    Column["Neo.timeline.Column"]
    Bars["Timeline bars<br/>inside matching rows"]

    Resources --> Grid
    Grid --> Column
    Events --> Column
    Axis --> Column
    Column --> Bars
```

The grid owns the rows. The event store supplies the intervals, and the time axis supplies their horizontal coordinates. The column projects the relevant events into each row.

Use a Timeline Column when you want a timeline alongside the other columns in an existing grid. Start with the [Resource Schedulers guide](Scheduler.md) when the central purpose of the view is a complete resource-booking experience with dedicated booking interactions. The two approaches share the timeline primitives; they serve different starting points.


## 2. A minimal grid with a Timeline Column

A working timeline needs a grid store containing resource rows, a `Neo.timeline.TimeAxis` defining the visible time range, and an event store containing dated records associated with those rows.

The following minimal viewport creates a grid with a resource column and a Timeline Column backed by a time axis and an
event store. Open Preview to run it here.

```javascript live-preview
import GridContainer  from '../grid/Container.mjs';
import TimeAxis       from '../timeline/TimeAxis.mjs';
import TimelineColumn from '../timeline/Column.mjs';
import EventStore     from '../timeline/store/Events.mjs';
import Viewport       from '../container/Viewport.mjs';

const resources = [
    {id: 'r-1', name: 'Design Team'},
    {id: 'r-2', name: 'Core Engine'},
    {id: 'r-3', name: 'QA & Testing'}
];

const events = [
    {
        id: 'ev-1',
        resourceId: 'r-1',
        title: 'Sprint Planning',
        startDate: '2026-11-16T08:00:00Z',
        endDate: '2026-11-16T11:00:00Z'
    },
    {
        id: 'ev-2',
        resourceId: 'r-2',
        title: 'Architecture Sync',
        startDate: '2026-11-16T09:00:00Z',
        endDate: '2026-11-16T12:00:00Z'
    },
    {
        id: 'ev-3',
        resourceId: 'r-3',
        title: 'Integration Tests',
        startDate: '2026-11-16T10:00:00Z',
        endDate: '2026-11-16T14:00:00Z'
    }
];

class MainViewport extends Viewport {
    static config = {
        className: 'Neo.examples.timeline.basic.Viewport',
        layout   : {ntype: 'fit'},
        items    : [{
            module   : GridContainer,
            rowHeight: 56,
            store    : {
                model: {fields: [{name: 'id'}, {name: 'name'}]},
                data : resources
            },
            columns: [
                {
                    dataField: 'name',
                    text     : 'Resource',
                    width    : 180,
                    locked   : 'start'
                },
                {
                    module   : TimelineColumn,
                    ntype    : 'timeline-header',
                    dataField: 'timeline',
                    text     : 'Schedule',
                    timeAxis : {
                        module     : TimeAxis,
                        start      : '2026-11-16T00:00:00Z',
                        end        : '2026-11-17T00:00:00Z',
                        timeZone   : 'UTC',
                        tickUnit   : 'hour',
                        tickStep   : 2,
                        pxPerMinute: 1
                    },
                    eventStore: {
                        module: EventStore,
                        data  : events
                    }
                }
            ]
        }]
    }
}

export default Neo.setupClass(MainViewport);
```

The resource store defines the grid rows, while the event store supplies the timeline bars. Each event's `resourceId` associates it with the corresponding resource row.

The Timeline Column is configured like any other grid column. Its `timeAxis` and `eventStore` configurations are converted into their corresponding Neo instances.

## 3. Events and rows

The resource store and event store answer different questions.

The grid's `store` determines which rows exist and provides the fields shown by ordinary columns. In the example, each resource has an `id` and a `name`.

The `eventStore` contains `Neo.timeline.model.Event` records. Each event has an identifier, a title, start and end dates, and a `resourceId` identifying its owning row. The model also supports `description`, `allDay`, `cls`, and `percentDone`.

By default, the column reads the row's `id` through `resourceIdField: 'id'`. It finds events whose `resourceId` matches that value. This means the event's `resourceId` must correspond to the resource key used by the row.

If your rows use a different key, set `resourceIdField` to its field name. For example, a grid whose resource records use `machineCode` can match event records by configuring `resourceIdField: 'machineCode'` and putting the corresponding machine code in each event's `resourceId`.

Several events can belong to the same row. When their time intervals overlap, Neo packs them into separate vertical lanes inside that row. Independent, non-overlapping intervals can use the same lane. This makes simultaneous work visible without placing one bar directly over another.

There is also a second data shape: an inline row record. When no `eventStore` is configured, the column checks the row itself for `startDate` and `endDate`. It can read the title and completion percentage from that same record as well. This is useful when each row represents one task or interval rather than a resource with multiple events.

The inline field names are configurable through `startDateField`, `endDateField`, `titleField`, and `percentDoneField`. The event-store approach is the natural fit when one resource row can own multiple independently managed events.

## 4. The time axis and its header

`Neo.timeline.TimeAxis` defines the temporal range and translates dates into horizontal positions. Its `start` and `end` establish the interval represented by the column.

The scale can be controlled with `pxPerMinute`: a higher value gives each minute more horizontal space. An explicit `size` can instead provide a fixed total width for the complete range. Choose a scale that makes the intervals readable without making the grid unnecessarily wide.

The axis also controls tick generation. `tickUnit` accepts `minute`, `hour`, `day`, `week`, or `month`; `tickStep` determines how many units separate ticks. In the example, `hour` with a step of `2` produces two-hour ticks.

Snapping controls editing precision, not the display frequency of the header ticks. `snapMinutes` sets the interval to which pointer-derived dates are snapped, relative to the time axis start. It defaults to 15 minutes; configure a different value when your application needs a coarser or finer editing interval. When an event is moved or resized, the drag zone converts the pointer position into a date and snaps it before calculating the updated interval.

Set `timeZone` deliberately when your application has a defined calendar zone. The example uses `UTC` and ISO timestamps ending in `Z`, so its event instants and axis calendar use the same reference. When no time zone is provided, the axis uses the viewer's local calendar.

The timeline header has two rows. The major row provides the broader time grouping, while the minor row displays the finer ticks. `majorTickUnit` and `majorTickStep` can override the major row's automatic unit, and `majorFormatter` and `minorFormatter` let you customize the corresponding labels. When no major unit is set, the header derives it from the axis tick unit.

For working calendars, the axis supports `nonWorkingDays` and `nonWorkingDates`. The default non-working weekdays are Sunday and Saturday; pass an empty array for `nonWorkingDays` when every weekday should count as working time. Set `showNonWorkingTime` on the Timeline Column to display the corresponding shaded ranges in its track and header.

## 5. Bars: content, styling, progress, and changes

Each event is represented by a bar positioned from its start and end dates. The default label comes from `titleField`, which uses `title` by default.

Use `barCls` to add a CSS class to the column's bars, or `cls` on an individual event to style that event differently. For more involved rendering, `barRenderer` receives a bar descriptor and a context containing the column and its virtual DOM node. It can return a replacement VDOM object or a string to use as the bar label.

When an event has a positive `percentDone` value, the column renders a progress fill inside the bar. Values are clamped to the `0..100` range for the fill width. `highlightedRecordIds` can mark selected event record IDs with the highlighted bar class.

Bar resizing is enabled by default through `resizableBars`. The column renders start and end handles, and the timeline drag zone handles moving and resizing intervals. On drop, the drag zone commits the pending dates through `owner.commitTimelineEdit()` when the owner provides it. Otherwise, it updates the event record with `record.set()` (or assigns the updated properties to a plain object) and asks the store to sort. A cancelled drag clears the pending drop, leaving the original record unchanged.

The [full basic Timeline example](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/examples/timeline/basic/Viewport.mjs) demonstrates the same data principle without a pointer gesture: its toolbar handler finds an event and calls `event.set()` with new `startDate` and `endDate` values. The store and grid continue to work with the updated record rather than a separate, manually maintained drawing.

## 6. Where to go next

To explore the complete implementation, including toolbar controls and record updates, see the [basic Timeline example source](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/examples/timeline/basic/Viewport.mjs).

For a complete resource-booking experience, continue with the [Building Resource Schedulers](Scheduler.md) guide. For hierarchical project plans with linked tasks, see [Gantt Charts & Linked Tasks](Gantt.md).

# [Gantt Charts & Linked Tasks](https://neomjs.com/raw/learn/guides/datahandling/Gantt.md)
Source: https://neomjs.com/learn/guides/datahandling/Gantt

---
seoTitle: "Building Gantt Charts with Linked Tasks | Neo.mjs"
seoDescription: "Learn how to build interactive Gantt charts with Neo.gantt.Container: hierarchical task trees, dependency records, cascade propagation, and working calendars."
---
# Building Gantt Charts with Linked Tasks

The `Neo.gantt.Container` is a specialized application component for scheduling, visualizing, and maintaining hierarchical work breakdowns across a continuous time axis. It extends `Neo.scheduler.Container` and unifies an interactive tree grid with a high-performance timeline that projects task durations, progress fills, milestones, and directed dependency linkages.

## 1. What a Gantt Chart Is in Neo.mjs

In the Neo.mjs architecture, a Gantt chart is not an ad-hoc visual overlay or an assortment of loosely tracked DOM elements. Instead, the chart is driven by two coordinated, observable data stores:

- **The Task Tree (`store`):** An instance of `Neo.gantt.TaskStore` (which extends `Neo.data.TreeStore`) holding hierarchical `Neo.gantt.TaskModel` records. Tasks form a tree structure representing project milestones, parent summary phases, and leaf work items.
- **The Dependency Graph (`dependencyStore`):** An instance of `Neo.gantt.DependencyStore` (extending `Neo.data.Store`) holding directed `Neo.gantt.DependencyModel` records. Each dependency links a predecessor task to a successor task.

Because `Neo.gantt.Container` inherits from `Neo.scheduler.Container` and `Neo.grid.Container`, the component splits its viewport into two synchronized views:
1. A locked tree column area defined by `taskColumns` (anchored to the start edge) that displays hierarchical task titles and attributes.
2. A timeline body governed by `timeAxis` that renders interactive task bars, milestones, and dependency vectors.

Every modification to either store—whether performed through mouse or touch gestures, inline cell editors, or direct record mutation—triggers reactive updates across both views.

## 2. A Minimal Chart

A functional Gantt chart can be mounted directly with inline configurations for tasks and dependencies. The minimal example below defines a parent summary phase with three sequential child tasks and Finish-to-Start dependencies:

```javascript
import DependencyStore from '../../../src/gantt/DependencyStore.mjs';
import Gantt           from '../../../src/gantt/Container.mjs';
import TaskStore       from '../../../src/gantt/TaskStore.mjs';
import Viewport        from '../../../src/container/Viewport.mjs';

const tasks = [
    {id: 'phase1', parentId: null,     isLeaf: false, collapsed: false, title: 'Phase 1: Foundation', startDate: '2026-11-09T00:00:00Z', endDate: '2026-11-14T00:00:00Z'},
    {id: 'task1',  parentId: 'phase1', isLeaf: true,  title: 'Site Survey',          startDate: '2026-11-09T00:00:00Z', endDate: '2026-11-10T00:00:00Z'},
    {id: 'task2',  parentId: 'phase1', isLeaf: true,  title: 'Architectural Blueprint', startDate: '2026-11-10T00:00:00Z', endDate: '2026-11-12T00:00:00Z'},
    {id: 'task3',  parentId: 'phase1', isLeaf: true,  title: 'Material Procurement',   startDate: '2026-11-12T00:00:00Z', endDate: '2026-11-14T00:00:00Z'}
];

const dependencies = [
    {id: 'dep-1-2', fromId: 'task1', toId: 'task2', type: 'FS', lag: 0, lagUnit: 'hour'},
    {id: 'dep-2-3', fromId: 'task2', toId: 'task3', type: 'FS', lag: 0, lagUnit: 'hour'}
];

class MainViewport extends Viewport {
    static config = {
        className: 'MyApp.view.MainViewport',
        layout   : {ntype: 'fit'},
        items    : [{
            module             : Gantt,
            reference          : 'gantt',
            editable           : true,
            rowHeight          : 56,
            store              : {module: TaskStore, data: tasks},
            dependencyStore    : {module: DependencyStore, data: dependencies},
            cascadeDependencies: true,
            taskColumns        : [{type: 'tree', dataField: 'title', text: 'Task Name', width: 220, locked: 'start'}],
            timeAxis           : {
                start      : '2026-11-09',
                end        : '2026-11-20',
                timeZone   : 'UTC',
                tickUnit   : 'day',
                pxPerMinute: 0.12,
                snapMinutes: 60
            },
            listeners: {
                taskChange: 'up.onTaskChange'
            }
        }]
    }

    onTaskChange(data) {
        // Handle persisted updates when tasks move or resize
    }
}

export default Neo.setupClass(MainViewport);
```

The `taskChange` listener receives `changeSource` for the edit origin (`keyboard`, `drag`, `resize`, `editor`, or the caller's `meta.source`, defaulting to `api`). Its `source` remains the Gantt's component id.

## 3. The Task Record

The data model for tasks is `Neo.gantt.TaskModel`. It extends `Neo.data.TreeModel` and incorporates timeline fields:

- **`id` (String | Number):** Unique record identifier.
- **`parentId` (String | Number | null):** References the parent task's `id`. Summary tasks at the root level specify `parentId: null`.
- **`isLeaf` (Boolean):** Set to `false` for parent phases and `true` for individual work packages.
- **`collapsed` (Boolean):** Controls the expansion state of child nodes in the tree column (defaults to `false`).
- **`startDate` & `endDate` (Date | String):** ISO date strings or Date objects specifying the start and completion instants.
- **`duration` (Number) & `durationUnit` (String):** Explicit span length (defaults to `'hour'`).
- **`milestone` (Boolean):** When `true`, indicates a point-in-time milestone rendered as a round marker rather than an extended bar.
- **`percentDone` (Number):** Completion percentage from `0` to `100`, visually rendered as an interior progress fill on the task bar.

Tasks are moved and updated through the chart so that dependencies cascade and change events fire. For example, moving a task by one day:

```javascript
gantt.moveTask('task1', {
    startDate  : '2026-11-10T00:00:00Z',
    endDate    : '2026-11-11T00:00:00Z',
    percentDone: 45
});
```

A direct write on a record (`task.set(...)`) updates that record's data directly, but bypasses the cascade engine and fires no `taskChange` event.

Because `TaskStore` is a hierarchical tree store, a parent folds through `gantt.store.collapse('phase1')` and opens through `gantt.store.expand('phase1')`, automatically toggling child row visibility in both the grid and timeline areas.

To let the tasks determine when a phase starts and finishes, set `rollupParents: true` on the task store.
Every chart sharing the store then sees the same phase dates. The earliest leaf starts the phase and the
latest leaf finishes it, including tasks inside collapsed or filtered branches. Each leaf contributes to
the phase's progress in proportion to its elapsed duration. A two-day task at 100% and a one-day task at
10% give the phase 70% completion, even if the tasks are separated by a week.

Move or resize a leaf to change the phase. An outgoing finish-to-start link uses the resulting phase finish
in the same chart edit. A derived phase supplies its own dates, so use a leaf as the destination of a new
dependency. Keep the store policy at its default of `false` for plans with independently scheduled parent
dates or an application-owned schedule service.

### Sharing tasks with a Scheduler and a Task Board

Folding a phase should hide its bars in the Gantt while its crew still sees their bookings. Give the
Gantt the full task tree and borrow its flat view of leaf records for the other two components:

```javascript
const bookings = gantt.store.getBookingStore();
scheduler.eventStore = bookings;
board.store = bookings;
```

The booking view has its own filters. Its records keep their identity when a phase is collapsed,
a task changes person, or a pane moves into another window. Add and remove tasks through the
owning task store. For date edits that must also reschedule a successor, use the same
`gantt.moveTask()` operation from either timeline. [One plan, three windows](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/examples/dashboard/planning/Workspace.mjs)
shows the wiring and the Scheduler's edit handler.

## 4. The Dependency Record

Precedence constraints between tasks are defined by `Neo.gantt.DependencyModel` records in `dependencyStore`. Each dependency specifies:

- **`id`:** Unique record identifier for the dependency link.
- **`fromId`:** Identifier of the predecessor task.
- **`toId`:** Identifier of the successor task.
- **`type`:** Precedence constraint type (`'FS'`, `'SS'`, `'FF'`, `'SF'`). Defaults to `'FS'`.
- **`lag`:** Signed numeric offset (defaults to `0`).
- **`lagUnit`:** Measurement unit for lag (`'minute'`, `'hour'`, `'day'`). Defaults to `'minute'`.

The cascade engine (`Neo.gantt.Cascade`) handles four relationship types:

| Link Type | Name | Successor Constraint | Real-World Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`FS`** | Finish-to-Start | Successor starts at or after predecessor completion (+ lag). | Standard sequential tasks: building walls begins after pouring foundation. |
| **`SS`** | Start-to-Start | Successor starts at or after predecessor start (+ lag). | Parallel workflows: structural inspection begins when excavation begins. |
| **`FF`** | Finish-to-Finish | Successor finishes at or after predecessor finish (+ lag). | Coordinated delivery: documentation writing finishes when QA testing finishes. |
| **`SF`** | Start-to-Finish | Successor finishes at or after predecessor start (+ lag). | Shift handovers: the legacy operations team departs when the new shift arrives. |

Dependencies can also be added or removed programmatically:

```javascript
gantt.dependencyStore.add({
    id     : 'dep-survey-arch',
    fromId : 'task1',
    toId   : 'task2',
    type   : 'FS',
    lag    : 4,
    lagUnit: 'hour'
});
```

A positive `lag` creates mandatory downtime between tasks, while a negative lag represents lead time where the successor starts prior to predecessor completion.

## 5. The Cascade

The cascade subsystem (`Neo.gantt.Cascade`) maintains schedule integrity whenever task dates change:

- **Automated Propagation:** When `cascadeDependencies: true` (the default setting), an edit through the chart (dragging a bar, the editor, keyboard navigation, or `gantt.moveTask()`) triggers downstream topological recomputation. Successors shift forward to respect incoming constraints or shift backward if preceding tasks conclude ahead of schedule. A direct write on a record (`task.set(...)`) changes that record only without triggering a cascade.
- **Manual Scheduling:** Setting `cascadeDependencies: false` disables automated propagation. Predecessor adjustments leave successor dates unchanged, allowing manual timeline adjustments.
- **Cycle Detection:** When computing required dates, `Cascade` inspects incoming edges. If a circular loop is encountered, cycles are detected and broken in discovery order.
- **Transitions:** With `animateCascade: true`, the bars a cascade changed travel from their previous to their final dates instead of jumping, and their links travel with them: bars and links read one in-flight span per task, stepped on one clock in the App Worker (`Neo.gantt.CascadeMotion`). A dragged or resized task stays where its preview dropped it while its successors travel. The move takes the theme's `--motion-panel` duration with `--ease-out-soft`, read from the chart's node when the transition is switched on, when the chart mounts and after each move. Reduced motion collapses that tier to `0ms`, so the cascade lands in one update, as it does while no read has answered. A scroll, a zoom, a store load, filter or sort, and the next edit land a running move at once; binding another store drops it. The records hold their final dates from the start, so `taskChange` listeners and `moveTask()` callers read the outcome immediately.

When a cascade completes, it returns an array of mutation descriptors:

```javascript
// Structure of cascaded adjustments emitted by Cascade
[
    {
        record      : taskRecord,
        dependencyId: 'dep-1-2',
        startDate   : nextStartDate,
        endDate     : nextEndDate,
        changes     : {startDate: nextStartDate, endDate: nextEndDate},
        previous    : {startDate: prevStartDate, endDate: prevEndDate}
    }
]
```

In the chart above, advancing `Site Survey` by 24 hours automatically causes `Architectural Blueprint` and `Material Procurement` to shift forward by 24 hours in sequence. Disabling `cascadeDependencies` retains downstream tasks at their existing dates.

## 6. Working Time & Calendars

Real-world schedules frequently observe non-working days such as weekends and holidays:

- **`useWorkingTime: true`:** When enabled (defaults to `false`), durations and lags calculate against the calendar of `Neo.timeline.TimeAxis`.
- **`nonWorkingDays`:** An array of day indices on `timeAxis` (defaults to `[0, 6]` for Saturday and Sunday).
- **Calendar Adjustments:** When active, tasks and lags that cross non-working intervals automatically stretch across the calendar without shortening the allocated working hours.
- **Snapping:** Using `snapMinutes` ensures tasks align cleanly to shifts or hour boundaries.

## 7. Interactive Links & Next Steps

`Neo.gantt.Container` provides direct gesture interaction for creating and adjusting links:

- **`dependencyCreation: true`:** Enables interactive link drag handles on task bars. Users can click and drag from the edge of a predecessor task to connect to a successor task. This configuration can also be supplied as a filter function `(from, to) => Boolean` where both arguments are task records (with `to` being `null` while only the start of a prospective link is tested) to enforce domain-specific link rules.
- **`schedule` Service:** An application can lend the chart a schedule service via the `schedule` config. The service decides and writes task edits and links itself, and can accept, defer, or refuse changes.

To inspect a complete application with local persistence, zoom presets, and interactive toolbar controls, see the [Gantt Basic Example source](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/examples/gantt/basic/Viewport.mjs). For related data patterns, explore the guides for [Grids](Grids.md) and [TreeStore](TreeStore.md).

# [Kanban Boards](https://neomjs.com/raw/learn/guides/datahandling/Board.md)
Source: https://neomjs.com/learn/guides/datahandling/Board

---
seoTitle: "Building Kanban Boards | Neo.mjs"
seoDescription: "Learn how to build a kanban board with Neo.board.Container: columns projected from one store, swimlanes, card moves through moveCard, card items, and long columns."
---
# Building Kanban Boards

The `Neo.board.Container` (`ntype: 'board'`) shows the records of one store as cards in columns and, optionally,
in swimlanes. It extends `Neo.container.Base`. The board owns no card state of its own: the records are the truth,
and the columns are a view of them.

## 1. What a Board Is in Neo.mjs

A board is not a set of hand-built lists that you keep in sync. It is a projection of one `Neo.data.Store`:

- **A card is a record:** Each card renders one record of the board's `store`, usually a `Neo.board.CardModel`.
- **A column is a query:** A column holds the records whose `statusField` (default `'status'`) equals the column's
  `status`, sorted by `orderField` (default `'order'`).
- **A move is one record change:** Dragging a card, moving it with the keyboard, saving it in the card editor, or
  calling `moveCard()` from code all end in one `record.set()` that writes the new status and order together.

Because the move is a record change, every other view bound to the same store follows it with no wiring. The
[board example](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/examples/board/basic/Viewport.mjs) shows this: a board and a
grid both bind the same store through a state provider, and a card dragged to another column updates the grid row of
that record.

## 2. A Minimal Board

A working board needs a store of cards and, optionally, the list of its columns:

```javascript
import Board     from '../../../src/board/Container.mjs';
import CardModel from '../../../src/board/CardModel.mjs';
import Viewport  from '../../../src/container/Viewport.mjs';

const cards = [
    {id: 1, title: 'Design the login form', status: 'backlog',     tags: ['ux']},
    {id: 2, title: 'Build the search box',  status: 'backlog',     tags: ['frontend']},
    {id: 3, title: 'Review the export',     status: 'in-progress', tags: ['qa'],   assignees: ['Avery'], progress: 40},
    {id: 4, title: 'Test the settings',     status: 'in-progress', tags: ['qa'],   assignees: ['Blake'], progress: 70},
    {id: 5, title: 'Ship the onboarding',   status: 'done',        tags: ['docs'], assignees: ['Casey'], progress: 100}
];

class MainViewport extends Viewport {
    static config = {
        className: 'MyApp.view.MainViewport',
        layout   : {ntype: 'fit'},
        items    : [{
            module   : Board,
            reference: 'board',
            store    : {model: CardModel, data: cards},
            columns  : [
                {status: 'backlog',     title: 'Backlog'},
                {status: 'in-progress', title: 'In progress', wipLimit: 2},
                {status: 'done',        title: 'Done'}
            ]
        }]
    }
}

export default Neo.setupClass(MainViewport);
```

The cards have no `order` yet. When the board first projects, it gives every record without a numeric order one
inside its column, in store order, so a fresh data set needs nothing extra.

`Neo.board.CardModel` declares the fields the board and its default card items read: `id`, `title`, `description`,
`status`, `lane`, `order`, `assignees`, `tags`, `progress`, `color` and `dueDate`. You may bring your own model
instead. The board reads the field names it needs from `statusField`, `orderField` and `laneField`, so a model with a
`state` field works with `statusField: 'state'`.

To share the store with other views, put it on a state provider and bind it. This excerpt is from the example's
`Viewport.mjs`:

```javascript
stateProvider: {
    module: StateProvider,
    stores: {cards: {module: MainStore}}
},

items: [{
    module: BoardContainer,
    bind  : {store: 'stores.cards'},
    columns
}]
```

## 3. Columns

There are two ways to get columns:

- **Derived:** With `columns: null` (the default), the board creates one column per distinct status value in the
  store, in first-seen order, titled by the status itself.
- **Explicit:** A `columns` array fixes the order and the titles, and keeps a column on screen even while it has no
  cards.

Each entry of `columns` takes `status` and, optionally:

| Config | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | the status | The header text. |
| `wipLimit` | `null` | A work-in-progress limit. The header badge shows `count/limit`, and a count above the limit marks the column with `neo-board-column-wip-exceeded`. Drops are not blocked. |
| `collapsed` | `false` | Hides the body and narrows the column to its header and count. A collapsed column stays a drop target. Users toggle it from the header. |
| `color` | `null` | A CSS color for the column's accent. |
| `locked` | `false` | Keeps the column at its index: its header shows a lock glyph and cannot be dragged. |
| `maxRenderedCards`, `overscan`, `retainOffscreen` | `100`, `10`, `null` | See section 7. |

Users reorder unlocked columns by dragging their headers (`columnsResortable`, `true` by default). The board writes
the new order back to `columns` and fires `columnMove` with `{status, laneValue, fromIndex, toIndex}`. Code can do
the same with `board.moveColumn(fromIndex, toIndex)`.

```javascript
columns: [
    {status: 'backlog',     title: 'Backlog',     locked: true},
    {status: 'ready',       title: 'Ready'},
    {status: 'in-progress', title: 'In progress', wipLimit: 5},
    {status: 'review',      title: 'Review',      wipLimit: 3},
    {status: 'done',        title: 'Done',        collapsed: true}
]
```

### Column summaries

To see the value of work in each column, declare the amount on your card model and configure the board's
`columnSummary`. For example, a sales board can total the amount of its visible deals:

```javascript
class DealModel extends CardModel {
    static config = {
        className: 'MyApp.model.Deal',
        fields   : [{name: 'amount', type: 'Float'}]
    }
}

const boardConfig = {
    module: Board,
    store : {model: Neo.setupClass(DealModel), data: [
        {id: 1, title: 'North', status: 'backlog', amount: 1200},
        {id: 2, title: 'South', status: 'backlog', amount: 800}
    ]},
    columnSummary: {
        field    : 'amount',
        formatter: sum => `$${sum.toFixed(2)}`
    }
};
```

The Backlog summary is `$2000.00`. The board sums finite numeric values for each status and, when swimlanes are
enabled, each lane/status intersection. It uses records remaining after the current store filters, including cards
outside the rendered window. An empty column sums to zero. The
formatter returns plain text for the header.

## 4. Swimlanes

Swimlanes add a second axis. Set `laneField` to the record field that names a card's lane, and the board switches
from one row of columns to one `Neo.board.LaneRow` per lane, each holding the full set of columns:

```javascript
{
    module   : Board,
    store    : {model: CardModel, data: cards},
    columns,
    laneField: 'lane',
    lanes    : [
        {value: 'web',    title: 'Web'},
        {value: 'mobile', title: 'Mobile', collapsed: true}
    ]
}
```

- **`lanes`:** Optional. Without it (`null`), the board derives one lane per distinct `laneField` value in first-seen
  order. With it, the listed lanes come first in that order, and any value the list does not name still gets a row
  after them. Each entry takes `value`, `title` and `collapsed`.
- **The unassigned lane:** Records whose lane value is `null` or missing land in one extra row with `value: null`,
  titled by `emptyLaneTitle` (`'Unassigned'` by default).

`CardModel` declares `lane` with a default of `null`, so a store that never sets it shows the unassigned lane only.
With `laneField: null` (the default), the board is a single row.

## 5. Moving Cards

All moves go through one method, `moveCard()`. The drag zone, the keyboard, the card editor and an agent all call it,
so a move from any source behaves the same.

- **Drag:** `dragResortable` (`true` by default) lets users drag cards within a column and across columns and lanes.
  It is independent of `columnsResortable`.
- **The keyboard:** `Neo.board.SelectionModel` is on by default. `Up`, `Down`, `Home` and `End` move the focus inside
  a column, and `Left` and `Right` move it to the nearest open column that holds cards. `Space` toggles selection, `Shift+Up` and
  `Shift+Down` extend it, `Ctrl+A` selects the column and `Escape` clears it. `Ctrl+Up`, `Ctrl+Down`, `Ctrl+Left` and
  `Ctrl+Right` move the focused card.
- **Code and agents:** Call `moveCard()` with the record (or its `key`, or the `cardId` of its card) and the target:

```javascript
// Inside the viewport of section 2: `reference: 'board'` finds the board
const board = this.getReference('board');

// To the top of "Done"
board.moveCard({key: 5, status: 'done', index: 0});

// In front of card 3, writing another field in the same set
board.moveCard({key: 1, status: 'in-progress', beforeId: 3, fields: {assignees: ['Devon']}});
```

The target position resolves from `beforeId`, then `afterId`, then `index`. Without any of them, the card goes to the
end of the column. `status` defaults to the record's current status, so a call with only `index` reorders the card
inside its column. With lanes, `lane` picks the target lane, `lane: null` picks the unassigned lane, and leaving it
out keeps the current one. The method returns the moved record, or `null` when the record or the target column does
not exist.

An agent on the Neural Link calls the same method on the board, addressing the card by key. Board ids are stable
(`<board>__col__<status>`, with `__<lane>` added when lanes are on, and `<board>__card__<key>`), so no index is
needed:

```javascript
call_method(boardId, 'moveCard', [{key: 5, status: 'review', index: 0}])
```

To react to moves, listen to the board's events:

```javascript
listeners: {
    cardMove({record, from, to}) {
        console.log(`${record.title}: ${from.status} -> ${to.status} at ${to.index}`);
    },
    cardsMove({records, status}) {
        console.log(`${records.length} cards dropped on ${status}`);
    },
    selectionChange({records}) {
        console.log(`${records.length} cards selected`);
    }
}
```

`cardMove` fires after each `moveCard()` with the `changes`, the `previous` values and both ends (`from` and `to`,
each `{status, lane, index}`). When several selected cards are dropped together, each one fires `cardMove`, and `cardsMove` then fires once with
`{records, status, laneValue}`.

## 6. What a Card Shows

`cardItems` lists what every card renders, in order. The default is
`[{type: 'title'}, {type: 'tags'}, {type: 'progress'}, {type: 'dueDate'}, {type: 'avatars'}]`. The built-in types are:

- `title`: the title line (field `title`).
- `text`: any text field; set `field`.
- `tags`: tag chips (field `tags`).
- `progress`: a bar over a 0 to 100 value (field `progress`). No value, or zero, draws no bar.
- `dueDate`: the due date as a `<time>` badge (field `dueDate`, an ISO date string or `Date`).
- `avatars`: the initials of each assignee (field `assignees`, names or objects with a `name`).

Each item may name another `field`. An item that finds nothing in its field renders nothing, so a backlog card
without assignees shows no empty avatar row. A record's `color` paints the card's accent.

```javascript
cardItems: [
    {type: 'title'},
    {type: 'text', field: 'description'},
    {type: 'avatars'}
]
```

To add a type of your own, register a renderer with `registerCardItem(type, renderer)` from
`src/board/CardItems.mjs`. The renderer receives `(record, item, card)` and returns one vdom node, or `null`.

**The card editor:** Double-clicking a card or pressing `Enter` on the focused card fires `cardActivate` with
`{card, record}` and opens the board's one shared `Neo.board.CardEditor` dialog. The card's menu button opens the same
dialog. The form follows
the board's model: it builds the fields the model declares (title and status always). Saving writes all changed
fields in one `record.set()`, and a changed status or lane goes through `moveCard()`, so the card lands at the end of
its new column. Cancel or `Escape` writes nothing. Double-clicking the title alone, or pressing `F2`, edits the title
inline. Code opens the editor with `board.openCardEditor(recordOrKey)`, and `cardEditorConfig` passes options, such
as the `fields` to show:

```javascript
cardEditorConfig: {fields: ['title', 'status', 'assignees']}
```

## 7. Long Columns

A column with many cards does not render them all. Each column renders a window of its records and creates more cards
as the user scrolls:

- **`maxRenderedCards`** (default `100`): when a column holds more records than this, it renders a window of that
  size. `null` renders every card.
- **`overscan`** (default `10`): extra cards rendered with the window, in total, so scrolling does not show gaps.
- **`retainOffscreen`** (default `null`): how many offscreen cards a sliced column keeps alive; `null` keeps up to one
  window.

All three are column configs, so they go on the entries of `columns`:

```javascript
columns: [
    {status: 'backlog', title: 'Backlog', maxRenderedCards: 50, overscan: 20},
    {status: 'done',    title: 'Done',    maxRenderedCards: null}
]
```

A record outside the window has no card, so `board.getCard(key)` returns `null` for it. The record is still in the
store: `moveCard({key})` still moves it, and `column.scrollToRecord(key)` brings it into view. Selection and keyboard
focus follow record keys, so they survive the scrolling too.

## 8. Where to Go Next

To see a sprint board with WIP limits and a grid that shares its store, read the
[Board Basic Example source](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/examples/board/basic/Viewport.mjs) and its
[store](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/examples/board/basic/MainStore.mjs).

For related component families:
- The [Resource Schedulers guide](Scheduler.md) applies the same idea, one store and an edit that is a record change,
  to bookings on a time axis.
- The [Gantt Charts & Linked Tasks guide](Gantt.md) adds task trees and dependency links on top of the scheduler.
- The [Using data.Store guide](UsingStores.md) and the [State Providers guide](StateProviders.md) cover the store and
  how several views bind one.

# [Tables (Stores)](https://neomjs.com/raw/learn/guides/datahandling/Tables.md)
Source: https://neomjs.com/learn/guides/datahandling/Tables

# Tables (Stores)

A task board starts with three rows. Then someone asks for an “open tasks” view, a priority order, an editor,
and a count that stays correct when a task is completed. The difficult part is no longer drawing the rows.
It is deciding which object owns the data, which objects merely present it, and what an edit should change.

`Neo.data.Store` is that data owner. It combines the ordered, keyed collection with a Model-defined record
population, change notifications, and a loading lifecycle. A table or grid displays the Store; it does not
have to become a second database. This separation lets you change the presentation while keeping the
record identities and data operations in one place.

“Tables” here means tabular application data. `Neo.table.Container` is a UI component that can display it.
A Store itself has no DOM: the same data can feed a table, a grid, a chart, or a picker.

For a complete practical workflow with a Store subclass, JSON loading and a shared Grid/ComboBox,
continue with [Using data.Store](#/learn/guides/datahandling/UsingStores).

## Give the rows a home

Three pieces cooperate. A **Model** describes the fields and their conversions. A **record** holds one
row's values using the accessors generated for that Model. A **Store** manages those records as a
collection and announces changes to its consumers. Records are lightweight objects; they are not
instances of `Neo.data.Model` or `Neo.core.Base`.

That distinction matters when a user edits a row. Replacing a plain array of display objects gives every
consumer another copy to reconcile. Editing a Store record preserves the object that the data layer
already knows, and its field setters notify the owning Store. A view can then react to the change without
being responsible for the field schema or transport.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Raw[Local data or a Pipeline response] --> Store[Store owns the record collection]
    Model[Model defines fields and conversion] --> Store
    Store --> Rows[Records carry row values and identity]
    Rows --> View[Table or grid presents the rows]
    View --> Edit[An edit changes a record field]
    Edit --> Notify[Owning Store publishes the change]
    Notify --> View
```

The [Records guide](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Records) explains field conversion and calculated values.
[Collections](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Collections) explains the underlying keys, ordering, filters,
and sorters. The Store is where those capabilities meet the application's data lifecycle.

## One dataset, two questions

Consider a list containing “Write,” “Review,” and “Archive.” An editor needs all three records; a work queue
needs only the unfinished ones, ordered by priority. Copying the unfinished records into another array
would make it easy for the editor and queue to disagree about the same task.

A `sourceId` projection offers a different arrangement: it keeps its own membership and order while
sharing record objects with the source. The following example runs inside an engine module; the relative
imports assume a module under `examples/your-app/`.

```javascript readonly
import Model from '../../src/data/Model.mjs';
import Store from '../../src/data/Store.mjs';

class TaskModel extends Model {
    static config = {
        className: 'MyApp.model.Task',
        fields: [
            {name: 'id',       type: 'Integer'},
            {name: 'title',    type: 'String'},
            {name: 'done',     type: 'Boolean'},
            {name: 'priority', type: 'Integer'}
        ]
    }
}
TaskModel = Neo.setupClass(TaskModel);

const tasks = Neo.create(Store, {
    model: TaskModel,
    data: [
        {id: 1, title: 'Write',   done: false, priority: 2},
        {id: 2, title: 'Review',  done: false, priority: 1},
        {id: 3, title: 'Archive', done: true,  priority: 0}
    ]
});
await tasks.ready();

const openTasks = Neo.create(Store, {
    model   : TaskModel,
    sourceId: tasks.id,
    filters : [{property: 'done', value: false}],
    sorters : [{property: 'priority', direction: 'ASC'}]
});
await openTasks.ready();

const ids = store => store.items.map(record => record.id);

console.log(ids(tasks));                      // [1, 2, 3]
console.log(ids(openTasks));                  // [2, 1]
console.log(tasks.get(1) === openTasks.get(1)); // true
console.log(tasks.count, openTasks.count);    // 3, 2
```

The priority order belongs to `openTasks`. It has not rearranged the source. The strict equality check is
the other half of the contract: these are two ways of finding the same record, not two independently
editable copies.

Reuse the **Model class**, as above, or provide separate Model configurations. Do not pass the same Model
instance into both Stores: a Model's `storeId` identifies the Store that receives its record changes.
`sourceId` does not inherit a Model configuration for you.

## A shared value is not a broadcast

There is a subtle boundary worth seeing before building a screen around it. Change Write's priority:

```javascript readonly
tasks.get(1).set({priority: 0});

console.log(openTasks.get(1).priority); // 0: it is the same record
console.log(ids(openTasks));          // [2, 1]: the projection has not re-sorted

openTasks.filter();
console.log(ids(openTasks));          // [1, 2]

tasks.get(1).done = true;
openTasks.filter();
console.log(tasks.count, openTasks.count); // 3, 1
console.log(ids(openTasks));               // [2]
```

These results were exercised against the Store implementation: changing the shared value was immediate,
but the queue's order changed only when its projection was refreshed. `sourceId` listens to source
collection mutations. It does **not** automatically forward every `recordChange` notification to every
derived Store. In this example, `filter()` explicitly recomputes membership and applies the configured
sorters, giving the queue its new result.

That is a design choice for the consumer to make deliberately. When multiple views should present exactly
the same live collection, bind them to the **same Store instance**. When each needs independent filters or
ordering, give the projection an explicit refresh path for the edits it must observe. A projection is
also not a read-only copy: collection mutations can propagate back to its source.

Within the owning Store, filters and sorters can opt into reevaluation after record edits using
`reapplyOnRecordChange: true`. The default is false. `autoSort: true` alone does not mean that every
ordinary field edit rearranges the collection. See
[Collections](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Collections) for the underlying filtering and sorting operations.
The record-edit opt-ins still require a notification: setting them on a projection does not forward a
source record change to it.

## Put the Store behind a view

Once the data has a home, the table's job gets small. Its columns select record fields through `dataField`,
and its `store` config points to the data it should show. It can display all tasks or the open-task
projection without owning the query logic.

For a screen with several consumers, put the Store in the view-root State Provider and bind the table to
it. The [State Provider table example](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/examples/stateProvider/table/MainContainer.mjs) uses this shape:

```javascript readonly
bind: {
    store: 'stores.main'
}
```

Here the provider creates and owns `stores.main`; the table receives that Store. Another view can bind to the same key.
The [State Providers guide](#/learn/guides/datahandling/StateProviders) shows the complete declaration and
binding setup. A [grid](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Grids) can use the same data-management approach when
the presentation needs virtualization.

Ownership also decides cleanup. In the standalone example above, the code that created the Stores should
destroy `openTasks` and then `tasks` when it is finished. A provider owns Stores it creates from
configurations or class references; it borrows Store instances passed in already constructed. Their
original owner remains responsible for disposal. Keeping that decision explicit prevents one consumer
from unexpectedly retiring the data another consumer still uses.

## Loading changes what “all rows” means

Local data makes the first example easy to reason about: all three records are already present. A server
introduces a second question: does the Store hold the whole dataset, or only the page the server returned?
A local filter can only judge the records the application actually has.

This is why counts need names. `count` is the Store's current visible membership. When a local filter is
active, `allItems` retains the unfiltered local population. `totalCount` is transport-supplied total
metadata; it is not a second spelling of `count`. In the local example, `tasks.count` is 3 while
`tasks.totalCount` is 0. Neither number establishes how many rows exist on a remote service.

`Store.load()` obtains data through its Pipeline, API, or URL configuration. `autoLoad` defaults to false,
so an application can decide when to start that work. Pipeline loads clear the previous rows unless
appending. For a Pipeline or API continuation, use `load({append: true})`. Appending does not advance
`currentPage`: the caller still selects the next page or cursor according to its service's contract.

For server-owned queries, `remoteFilter` and `remoteSort` send the relevant query configuration through
the load path, and `pageSize` participates in the request. They do not give a client-only Store knowledge
of rows it has never received. Choose local operations for a locally owned population and remote
operations when the service owns the complete query result.

The [Data Pipelines guide](#/learn/guides/datahandling/DataPipelines) owns transport configuration, parsing,
and normalization. [Streaming](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Streaming) explains progressive arrivals.
Those are different loading strategies for the same data owner, rather than separate data models for
each view.

One event detail prevents a misleading spinner: the Store's `load` event also announces local data
changes such as sorting. It is not proof that a network request just completed. `isLoadPending` tracks
outstanding `load()` invocations; progressive data can already be visible while that signal remains true.
A screen can show request feedback without hiding the rows it has already received.

The payoff is a screen whose data responsibilities remain visible: the Model defines a row, the Store
owns the population and its lifecycle, an explicit projection answers a narrower question, and the view
presents the answer. Adding another view no longer requires inventing another owner for the same data.

---

# [Using data.Store](https://neomjs.com/raw/learn/guides/datahandling/UsingStores.md)
Source: https://neomjs.com/learn/guides/datahandling/UsingStores

# Using data.Store

A location picker and a grid can begin with the same list and still have different jobs. Someone types
“Arizo” into the picker to find Arizona; the grid should continue showing the whole catalog. Then an edit
changes Arizona's display name, and the grid should repaint from the source notification. Closing the
picker should not stop the grid from receiving later edits.

Those are data ownership questions before they are rendering questions. Copying arrays between the two
components gives you two populations to keep synchronized. A `Neo.data.Store` lets the application own
one population, while each component presents or queries it for its own purpose.

This walkthrough builds that arrangement: a Model and Store class, a shared Grid/ComboBox view, a real
JSON load, and an application-owned shortlist. The [Tables (Stores) guide](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Tables)
explains the underlying ownership model; here we put it to work. `Store` extends `collection.Base`, adding
Model-defined records, loading and record-change notifications. Its records are row objects created from
the Model's schema, not instances of the Model class.

## Give every row a stable key

A row's array position is a poor identity. Sorting can move Arizona without making it a different place.
Use its abbreviation as the key, and a lookup can continue to mean the same thing after sorting or filtering.

The following modules assume an example folder such as `examples/my-store-guide/` in the Engine
repository. Adjust the Engine import paths for your own application. Save this first module as
`StatesStore.mjs`:

```javascript readonly
import Model from '../../src/data/Model.mjs';
import Store from '../../src/data/Store.mjs';

class StateModel extends Model {
    static config = {
        className  : 'StoreGuide.model.State',
        keyProperty: 'abbreviation',
        fields     : [
            {name: 'abbreviation', type: 'String'},
            {name: 'name',         type: 'String'}
        ]
    }
}
StateModel = Neo.setupClass(StateModel);

class StatesStore extends Store {
    static config = {
        className  : 'StoreGuide.store.States',
        keyProperty: 'abbreviation',
        model      : StateModel,
        data       : [
            {abbreviation: 'AZ', name: 'Arizona'},
            {abbreviation: 'CA', name: 'California'},
            {abbreviation: 'NY', name: 'New York'}
        ],
        sorters: [{property: 'name', direction: 'ASC'}]
    }
}
StatesStore = Neo.setupClass(StatesStore);

export {StateModel};
export default StatesStore;
```

The Model defines the fields and their conversions; the Store defines the population and its initial
ordering. Both agree on `abbreviation` as the key. A Store created from this class can therefore answer
`states.get('AZ')` directly, without searching display text or depending on a row index.

The [Records guide](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Records) goes deeper into field definitions and conversion.
[Collections](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Collections) owns the filtering and sorting vocabulary used here.
You do not need to reproduce those mechanisms in the view.

## Give two views one data owner

Put the Store in the State Provider at the root of the screen. The provider creates it once, and the Grid
and ComboBox bind to that instance. Save this complete view as `MainView.mjs` beside `StatesStore.mjs`:

```javascript readonly
import ComboBox    from '../../src/form/field/ComboBox.mjs';
import Grid        from '../../src/grid/Container.mjs';
import Provider    from '../../src/state/Provider.mjs';
import StatesStore from './StatesStore.mjs';
import Viewport    from '../../src/container/Viewport.mjs';

class MainView extends Viewport {
    static config = {
        className: 'StoreGuide.view.MainView',
        layout   : {ntype: 'vbox', align: 'stretch'},
        stateProvider: {
            module: Provider,
            stores: {states: StatesStore}
        },
        items: [{
            module       : ComboBox,
            reference    : 'chooser',
            labelText    : 'Find a location',
            labelPosition: 'top',
            valueField   : 'abbreviation',
            displayField : 'name',
            typeAhead    : false,
            bind         : {store: 'stores.states'}
        }, {
            module   : Grid,
            reference: 'grid',
            flex     : 1,
            bind     : {store: 'stores.states'},
            columns  : [
                {dataField: 'abbreviation', text: 'Code', width: 120},
                {dataField: 'name', text: 'Location', flex: 1}
            ]
        }]
    }
}

export default Neo.setupClass(MainView);
```

Use the exported class as your app's `mainView`. For an existing example shell, its `app.mjs` is:

```javascript readonly
import MainView from './MainView.mjs';

export const onStart = () => Neo.app({name: 'StoreGuide', mainView: MainView});
```

The view declares which fields to display; it does not manufacture another array of rows. The Grid
receives the source Store's membership and record-change signals through the Engine.

Try typing **Arizo** into the picker. Its result narrows to Arizona, while the grid retains its three
rows. A ComboBox given a Store instance already creates its own filtering view internally. You do not
need to build a second Store merely to stop the picker's query from filtering the grid.

Shared record identity also carries edits to both views. A source edit repaints the Grid, and the
ComboBox forwards it to its private picker view, so an already-open picker list shows the new label too.
An edit does not re-run the picker's query, though: a record whose new label no longer matches the typed
text stays listed until the next keystroke.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Provider[View-root State Provider] --> Source[One source Store]
    Model[Model class defines the row schema] --> Source
    Source --> Grid[Grid presents the source population]
    Source --> PickerView[ComboBox owns its private query view]
    PickerView --> Picker[Picker shows matching choices]
    Source --> Shortlist[Application-owned shortlist with its own query]
```

This distinction saves more than a filter configuration. The screen has one place to apply edits,
one source for the grid, and a clear owner when the screen is destroyed. The provider owns the Store it
created from the class reference. If you instead pass a pre-existing Store instance into a provider,
that instance is borrowed; its original owner remains responsible for it. See
[State Providers](#/learn/guides/datahandling/StateProviders) for the broader binding and lifecycle model.

## Replace the local sample with a JSON load

The same view can display remote data. Replace the provider's `stores` declaration with this descriptor:

```javascript readonly
stores: {
    states: {
        module  : StatesStore,
        data    : null,
        url     : new URL('../../resources/examples/data/us_states.json', import.meta.url).href,
        autoLoad: true
    }
}
```

The URL is resolved from `MainView.mjs` in the example folder specified above. It points to a real
repository resource; use your own endpoint in an application. Making this URL absolute also removes
ambiguity about whether a relative path belongs to the page, the App Worker or a packaged installation.

The `data: null` override matters. It clears the class's local sample without declaring a loaded dataset.
Even `data: []` is an explicit, already-loaded empty population, so the Store's construction path does
not start `autoLoad` for it. In testing this exact example, an empty array produced zero requests;
the distinction is about loaded state, not simply whether there are any rows.

The response carries the rows under `data`. A valid two-row response has this shape:

```json readonly
{
    "success": true,
    "data": [
        {"abbreviation": "AL", "name": "Alabama"},
        {"abbreviation": "AK", "name": "Alaska"}
    ]
}
```

The repository's full sample contains 59 entries, including territories. It is larger than the Grid's
visible row pool, so you can scroll while the Store continues to own the whole loaded population.
Only the Store descriptor changed; the columns and the picker still bind to `stores.states`.

Use the public configuration names `url` and `autoLoad` when creating a Store. Automatic loading is
optional. When a workflow needs to choose when a request starts, create the Store with `autoLoad: false`
and call `load()` deliberately:

```javascript readonly
const remoteStates = Neo.create(StatesStore, {
    data    : [],
    url     : new URL('../../resources/examples/data/us_states.json', import.meta.url).href,
    autoLoad: false
});
await remoteStates.ready();
await remoteStates.load();

console.log(remoteStates.get('AZ').name); // Arizona
```

`ready()` is the instance-initialization boundary; do not substitute it for completion of an automatically
started network request. `await load()` follows the load invocation you started. Request-pending state
and record availability are also different: progressive rows may be usable while `isLoadPending` is
still true. The [Data Pipelines guide](#/learn/guides/datahandling/DataPipelines) explains transport and
normalization, and [Streaming](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Streaming) covers progressive delivery.

The manual example can use `data: []` because its explicit `load()` starts the request; it does not rely
on the construction-time `autoLoad` decision.

## Edit the record, rather than replacing the screen's data

Inside a controller or other code that already owns a reference to `mainView`, obtain the same Store:

```javascript readonly
const states = mainView.stateProvider.getStore('states');

const onRecordChange = ({record, fields}) => {
    console.log(record.abbreviation, fields.map(field => field.name));
};
states.on('recordChange', onRecordChange);

states.get('AZ').name = 'Arizona — edited';

const [added] = states.add({abbreviation: 'AX', name: 'Aster sample'});
console.log(added === states.get('AX')); // true
states.remove(added);

states.un('recordChange', onRecordChange);
```

The field setter announces a record edit. `add()` and `remove()` change collection membership. The Grid
receives those signals from its Store; there is no second display array to rebuild or manually notify.
Keep structural mutations on the source when that source is the population your application owns.

I am Sophie, one of Neo's maintainers. While preparing this walkthrough, I exercised a less obvious
sequence than “type and pick”: edit a source record with the picker present, remove the picker, then edit
the same record again. The useful result was not just that both searches looked right. The source still
emitted `recordChange`, and the Grid still changed after the field was gone. That is the continuity your
screen needs when a filter panel, dialog or optional editor is removed during ordinary use.

There is one schema-ownership rule behind that result: **reuse the Model class, not a single Model
instance across independent Stores**. A Model instance carries a `storeId` notification route. Handing
that same instance to another Store can transfer the route away from the original owner. Passing
`StateModel`, as the examples do, lets each Store obtain its own instance of the same schema.

## Create a shortlist when the application owns another question

Sometimes a second query is part of the product: a work queue, a comparison set, or a shortlist shown
beside the full catalog. That is where an explicit `sourceId` Store is useful. It shares record objects
with the source while keeping its own filtering and order.

For the loaded sample, create a descending shortlist of names beginning with A. Import `Store` from the
Engine and the named `StateModel` export from `StatesStore.mjs` in the module running this code:

```javascript readonly
const shortlist = Neo.create(Store, {
    model      : StateModel,
    keyProperty: 'abbreviation',
    sourceId   : states.id,
    filters    : [{property: 'name', operator: 'startsWith', value: 'A'}],
    sorters    : [{property: 'name', direction: 'DESC'}]
});
await shortlist.ready();

console.log(shortlist.get('AZ') === states.get('AZ')); // true
console.log(shortlist.model === states.model);        // false
console.log(shortlist.items.map(record => record.abbreviation));
// ['AR', 'AZ', 'AS', 'AK', 'AL']
```

The descending order belongs to the shortlist. The source remains alphabetically ascending. Adding
`{abbreviation: 'AX', name: 'Aster sample'}` to the source adds the same new record to the shortlist;
removing it from the source removes that membership again. In the full sample, the counts move from
59 and 5 to 60 and 6, then back. The views are independent queries, not disconnected copies.

Shared identity alone does not make every edit a projection refresh. Change a field so a record no
longer matches the shortlist, then explicitly recompute its query:

```javascript readonly
const arizona = states.get('AZ');
arizona.name = 'Z — Arizona';

console.log(shortlist.count); // 5: membership has not been recomputed
shortlist.filter();
console.log(shortlist.count); // 4

arizona.name = 'Arizona';
shortlist.filter();
console.log(shortlist.count); // 5
```

If your application needs this refresh on each source edit, connect the source's `recordChange` event
to that policy explicitly and remove the listener when the consuming view ends. Do not assume that
setting an edit-refilter option on the derived Store forwards notifications it never receives. The
[Tables guide](#/learn/guides/datahandling/Tables) explains that boundary in more detail.

Finally, retire what you created. The root provider destroys its created Store when the view ends.
A standalone Store created by the code above is yours to destroy when its owner finishes. Destroying it
also lets go of the Model it created from the class reference, so there is no separate Model to dispose.
Release any source listeners you installed:

```javascript readonly
shortlist.destroy();
remoteStates.destroy();
```

The practical payoff is a screen that can grow without multiplying data owners. Keep one source for the
population, let components own their presentation queries, and introduce an explicit projection only
when the application has another question to answer. Then edits, loading and teardown have places to
belong, instead of becoming synchronization code scattered across every view.
