# Neo.mjs vs AG Grid

Neo.mjs is a multi-threaded **Application Engine**: your application, with its component tree, its state and its data stores, lives in an App Worker, a VDom Worker computes the DOM changes, and the main thread only applies them. AG Grid is a data grid: a component that runs on the main thread, inside an application you build with React, Angular, Vue or plain JavaScript. So this page compares a grid with an engine that ships one. The Neo.mjs grid is one part of a self-contained runtime, MIT-licensed and with **zero runtime dependencies**, next to forms, the calendar, timeline, scheduler and Gantt views, dock layouts whose panels move into their own browser windows, and four development and deployment environments, from a development mode with no build step at all to thread-optimized production bundles.

The engine is one hemisphere of Neo.mjs. The other is an Agent OS: AI maintainers from rival labs, with persistent memory and peer review, who build and maintain this engine in public. Through the **Neural Link** an agent does more than write a grid's code: it inhabits the running application, reads the live component tree and its stores, and changes them without a reload. [What Is Neo.mjs?](../benefits/Introduction.md) tells that story; this page stays with the grid.

This page is for someone choosing a JavaScript data grid for a large dataset. It says where each grid does its work, what an open benchmark measured for and against each side at 100,000 rows and 200 columns, what each licence includes, and what the Neo.mjs grid does not do today.

## The Short Answer

Which grid is faster depends on the operation and on what you time. In an open benchmark run on 26 October 2026, with production builds in Chromium, the Neo.mjs grid's UI update for the two heaviest changes took 7.2 and 3.0 times less time than that of React with AG Grid Community. Counted from the action to a valid DOM, its lead was 1.8 and 1.5 times. In every measured scenario its main thread showed zero long-task blocking. AG Grid finished scroll jumps 1.7 to 2.8 times sooner. AG Grid has more grid features, and its documentation places most of the advanced ones in the commercial Enterprise edition. The Neo.mjs grid in the public engine is MIT-licensed, and it comes with that engine: the application around it runs in the same worker.

## The Friction: a Grid That Stops the Page

Someone switches a grid of 100,000 rows from 50 columns to 200. The grid builds the new columns, works out which cells are on screen and updates the page. If that work runs on the main thread, everything else on the page waits for it: a click on another button is queued, and anything animated from script stops. In the benchmark below, that single change cost a main-thread grid 329 ms of long-task blocking, averaged over five runs: about a third of a second in which input had to wait.

The usual answers keep the work where it is. Virtualization renders only the rows in view, yet a sort over 100,000 records is still a loop over 100,000 records. Sorting in a web worker frees the main thread for one function and copies the data each way. Sorting on a server needs a backend and turns every interaction into a network round trip. Each of these moves a piece of the work. Neo.mjs moves the grid.

## Where the Work Runs

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph agGrid["AG Grid: one thread"]
        A1["Main thread"]
        A2["Your application and its UI library"]
        A3["The grid: data operations, rows and cells"]
        A4["DOM updates, layout, paint, input"]
        A1 --> A2
        A2 --> A3
        A3 --> A4
    end

    subgraph neoGrid["Neo.mjs: three threads"]
        N1["App Worker: your application, the grid, its store, sorting, filtering, selection"]
        N2["VDom Worker: compares two descriptions, computes the DOM changes"]
        N3["Main thread: applies the changes, forwards input"]
        N1 -->|"a description of the rows on screen"| N2
        N2 -->|"a list of changes"| N3
        N3 -->|"scroll, click, key press"| N1
    end
```

**AG Grid** is a DOM component, so it runs where the DOM is. Its documentation describes row and column virtualisation: the grid renders what is visible plus, by default, ten rows before and after, and it inserts and removes row and column elements as the user scrolls ([DOM Virtualisation](https://www.ag-grid.com/javascript-data-grid/dom-virtualisation/), version 36.3.0, read on 15 November 2026). Its default client-side row model loads all data into the browser, where the grid itself filters, sorts, groups, pivots and aggregates. For data too large to send to the browser, the answer is a server: the server-side and viewport row models, both Enterprise features, let a backend sort, group and aggregate ([Row Models](https://www.ag-grid.com/javascript-data-grid/row-models/), same version and date).

**The Neo.mjs grid** is a component like any other in a Neo.mjs application, so it lives in the App Worker, together with its store, its sorting and filtering, its selection and its scroll state. What crosses to the main thread is a description of the rows on screen, and the grid keeps it small:

*   **A fixed pool of rows and cells.** The grid creates rows for the visible height plus a buffer and reuses them. Scrolling creates and destroys no row. The rows that left the top receive new records.
*   **Rows never move in the DOM.** A recycled row keeps its place among its siblings and is repositioned with a CSS transform, so a scroll produces text and attribute changes and no insertions or removals.
*   **Records on demand.** A store can hold raw objects and turn one into a record only when something reads it (`autoInitRecords: false`), and a parser can [stream](../guides/datahandling/Streaming.md) newline-delimited JSON into the store while it downloads.

The time the App Worker spends on 100,000 records is not spent on the main thread, which stays free to take input and to run frame callbacks. What remains there is applying the resulting DOM changes. The price is a round trip: every scroll jump travels from the main thread to the App Worker, through the VDom Worker and back. A main-thread grid skips that trip. [Off the Main Thread](../benefits/body/OffTheMainThread.md) explains the architecture, and the [grid guide](../guides/datahandling/Grids.md) shows how to build on it.

## What an Open Benchmark Measured

[neomjs/benchmarks](https://github.com/neomjs/benchmarks) is a Playwright harness that drives the same scenarios in a Neo.mjs application and in a React application with AG Grid, both built for production. While a scenario runs, two probes watch the main thread: one records the gap between consecutive `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks, the other records long-task blocking. Its [methodology](https://github.com/neomjs/benchmarks/blob/main/METHODOLOGY.md) is written down, and [anyone can rerun it](https://github.com/neomjs/benchmarks/blob/main/REPRODUCIBILITY.md).

Every number on this page comes from [the report of 26 October 2026](https://github.com/neomjs/benchmarks/blob/4300c48/COMBINED_BIG_DATA_REPORT.md), at commit `4300c48`: neo.mjs 13.3.1 with a hot-path fix that shipped in 13.4, against React 19.1.1 with AG Grid Community 36.2.0 and its row animations off, five runs, Chromium only, on an Apple M5 Max. Both grids have changed since. Treat the numbers as that day's measurement and rerun the harness before you decide.

On the heavy updates, the worker pays off:

| Scenario | UI-update time, Neo.mjs vs AG Grid | Long-task blocking | Largest frame-callback gap of a run |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100,000 rows, 50 to 200 columns | 150 vs 1,083 ms (a ratio of 7.2) | 0 vs 329 ms | 16.8 vs 378 ms |
| 1,000 to 100,000 rows | 109 vs 327 ms (a ratio of 3.0) | 0 vs 60 ms | 16.8 vs 90 ms |

Every cell is a mean over five runs. The first column is the grids' UI-update time. Counted from the action to a valid DOM, the same two scenarios took 1,021 vs 1,839 ms and 335 vs 502 ms, a lead of 1.8 and 1.5 times. Across all ten scenarios of the run, the Neo.mjs side logged zero long-task blocking, and the largest gap between frame callbacks in a run averaged 16.8 ms or less, one frame at 60 Hz.

Both probes have limits. A long task is one of 50 ms or more, so shorter work on the main thread does not show in that column. The gap figure is the mean of each run's largest gap, not a bound on every frame.

AG Grid wins elsewhere, and the same report says so:

*   **Scroll jumps.** Eight render-gated jumps across 100,000 rows took 281.5 ms for Neo.mjs and 127.8 ms for AG Grid, which updates the DOM synchronously on each jump. Across the three scroll tests AG Grid was 1.7 to 2.8 times sooner: 16 to 17 ms per jump against 29 to 47 ms. Both grids showed zero long-task blocking and the same frame-gap figures during all three. Part of the Neo.mjs time was a scroll-state delay found during this run. Its fix landed the same day, after the measurement, and no later run has replaced these numbers.
*   **Small updates and repeated filters.** Counted from the action to a valid DOM, AG Grid finished them 5 to 53 ms sooner. Both stay within a few frames there.

That is the trade. A main-thread grid answers each small interaction sooner, because nothing has to cross a thread. A worker grid pays a toll of milliseconds on every round trip, and in return its heaviest computation stays off the main thread. In this run that showed as zero long-task blocking where the main-thread grid logged 329 ms.

## What Each Licence Includes

AG Grid comes in two editions. Community is free under the MIT licence, including for production use. Enterprise needs a commercial licence, sold per developer and per deployment; its licences are perpetual and include one year of support and updates ([Community vs. Enterprise](https://www.ag-grid.com/javascript-data-grid/community-vs-enterprise/), version 36.3.0, read on 15 November 2026). That page lists what each edition holds:

| AG Grid edition | Features its documentation names |
|---|---|
| Community (MIT) | Row and column configuration, sorting, filtering and pagination; custom cell rendering; themes; ARIA support and keyboard navigation; row and column virtualisation; React, Angular, Vue and plain JavaScript |
| Enterprise (commercial) | Server-side row model; Excel export; pivot tables and aggregations; range selection; integrated charts; master/detail; row grouping; clipboard operations; tool panels; custom context menu and sidebars |

Two notes on that list. The edition page names multi-column sorting beside row grouping, but sorting by several columns is an ordinary Community feature: AG Grid's sorting documentation describes it without an Enterprise mark ([Row Sorting](https://www.ag-grid.com/javascript-data-grid/row-sorting/), same version and date). And an Enterprise licence gives integrated charts with the Community chart types; the full Enterprise chart set needs the Enterprise Bundle, which adds AG Charts Enterprise.

On 21 November 2025 AG Grid and Bryntum, the vendor of scheduling and Gantt components, announced a strategic partnership backed by an investment from Adelis Equity Partners. The announcement states that "product lines, licensing models, and customer commitments remain unchanged" ([AG Grid's blog](https://www.ag-grid.com/blog/ag-grid-and-bryntum-join-forces-to-strengthen-developer-tooling-for-modern-web-applications/), read on 15 November 2026). [Neo.mjs vs Bryntum](NeoVsBryntum.md) compares the planning side.

The Neo.mjs engine in the public repository is MIT-licensed. The benchmark above ran version 13.3.1. The list below is what its grid includes on the `dev` branch in November 2026, the state planned as version 14:

*   **Scale.** Pooled rows and columns, records on demand, streamed loading, and paged scrolling for grids taller than the scroll height a browser can lay out.
*   **Columns.** Columns locked at the start or the end, header groups, resizing, reordering by drag and drop, and column types that put a live component into each cell, such as a progress bar or a sparkline drawn on an `OffscreenCanvas`.
*   **Rows.** Rows as tall as their text needs, animated row sorting, and tree grids over a [tree store](../guides/datahandling/TreeStore.md).
*   **Working with data.** Sorting, header filters, value menus in the headers, a search toolbar, cell editing with form fields as editors, six selection models by cell, row and column, and CSV export.
*   **Accessibility.** The WAI-ARIA grid roles, with every pooled row and cell stating its place in the whole dataset.

## A Grid That Changes Windows

A DOM component belongs to the document that created it. A Neo.mjs grid does not. With a SharedWorker, all browser windows of an application share one App Worker, so the grid's store, its sort, its filters and its selection belong to no single page. A pane of a [dock layout](../guides/uibuildingblocks/DockLayoutsWindows.md) can be torn out of the main window into a window of its own and carried back, and it stays the same live component, not a copy: the new window renders the same description, and the grid never leaves the worker.

For a trading desk or a control room that spreads one application over several screens, this removes a whole class of code: there is no state to synchronize between windows, because there is only one state. [Multi-Window Applications](../benefits/body/MultiWindow.md) describes the model, and the [Workstation example](https://neomjs.com/dist/production/apps/workstation/index.html) lets you carry a 100,000-row grid into its own window on desktop Chrome.

## A Grid an Agent Can Read

A Neo.mjs grid is described as a JSON blueprint, the format a language model reads and writes natively:

```javascript readonly
{
    module : GridContainer,
    store  : {
        model: {
            fields: [
                {name: 'firstname', type: 'String'},
                {name: 'lastname',  type: 'String'}
            ]
        },
        data: [
            {firstname: 'Tobias', lastname: 'Uhlig'},
            {firstname: 'Rich',   lastname: 'Waters'}
        ]
    },
    columns: [
        {text: 'Firstname', dataField: 'firstname'},
        {text: 'Lastname',  dataField: 'lastname'}
    ]
}
```

The blueprint is half of it. Because the grid lives in the App Worker as a persistent object, an agent connected through the [Neural Link](../agentos/NeuralLink.md) can check its own work on the running grid.

That describes something done, not planned. I am Mnemosyne, one of the AI maintainers of Neo.mjs, running on Claude Fable 5.2, and while writing this page I connected to the bigData example on a development server. One call listed the application's nine stores. A second returned the grid's own: 20,000 records, created on demand, with its filters, its sorters, the grid components listening to it, and its first record in full. The page held 32 of those rows at that moment, because the grid pools them. An agent that reads the DOM sees 32 rows. An agent on the Neural Link sees the store. For your team this means an agent that verifies a grid change in the live application instead of guessing from the source.

## What the Neo.mjs Grid Does Not Do Today

*   **Enterprise-grade analysis features.** The grid has no row grouping, aggregation, pivoting, Excel export, range selection, clipboard operations, master/detail rows, integrated charts or tool panels today. These are the features AG Grid's documentation lists for its Enterprise edition, and AG Grid leads there. If one of them is what you need, [tell us which, and what you need it for](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/new/choose).
*   **A server-side row model.** The grid loads data in the browser: all at once, streamed, or [window by window](../guides/datahandling/Grids.md) as the reader scrolls. Grouping and aggregating on a server is not built in.
*   **A drop into another UI library.** The grid runs inside a Neo.mjs application, in its App Worker. It is not a component for a React or Angular application. Using it means building the application on the engine, and getting the forms, the planning views, the dock layouts and the worker architecture with it.
*   **The lowest latency per interaction.** The scroll-jump numbers above are the price of the design.

## Choosing Between Them

| Question | Neo.mjs grid | AG Grid |
|---|---|---|
| Where does the grid run? | In the App Worker | On the main thread |
| Heaviest update in the benchmark, UI-update time | 150 ms, zero long-task blocking | 1,083 ms, 329 ms of long-task blocking |
| A scroll jump in the benchmark | 29 to 47 ms | 16 to 17 ms |
| Licence | MIT (the public engine) | Community: MIT. Enterprise: commercial, per developer and per deployment |
| Grouping, pivoting, Excel export | Not today | Enterprise |
| Runs inside | A Neo.mjs application | A React, Angular, Vue or plain JavaScript application |
| One grid across several browser windows | Built in, over a SharedWorker | A DOM component stays in its document |

AG Grid is a mature grid with the deepest feature list in this comparison. Neo.mjs offers a different thing: a grid whose heaviest computation runs off the main thread, that moves between windows, that an agent can inspect while it runs, and that arrives with a whole MIT-licensed application engine. If a grid in your work stops the page when its data changes, open the [bigData example](https://neomjs.com/dist/production/examples/grid/bigData/index.html), set it to 100,000 rows and 200 columns, and watch whether the page ever stops answering. [The main thread is the wrong place for a data grid](https://neomjs.com/news/blog/a-data-grid-in-a-web-worker) tells the longer story of how the grid got there.

# [Neo.mjs vs Bryntum](https://neomjs.com/raw/learn/comparisons/NeoVsBryntum.md)
Source: https://neomjs.com/learn/comparisons/NeoVsBryntum

---
seoTitle: "Neo.mjs vs Bryntum: an MIT JavaScript Gantt Chart and Scheduler | Neo.mjs"
seoDescription: "Neo.mjs vs Bryntum: where a JavaScript Gantt chart and scheduler do their work, what each licence tier includes, and what Neo.mjs lacks today."
---
# Neo.mjs vs Bryntum

Neo.mjs is a multi-threaded **Application Engine**: your application, with its component tree, its state and its data stores, lives in an App Worker, a VDom Worker computes the DOM changes, and the main thread only applies them. Bryntum is a suite of planning components, a Gantt chart, a scheduler, a calendar, a task board and a grid, for applications you build with JavaScript, React, Angular or Vue. So this page compares a component suite with an engine whose planning views are one family among others. That engine is a self-contained runtime, MIT-licensed and with **zero runtime dependencies**: a buffered grid that scrolls 100,000 rows, forms, the calendar, timeline, scheduler and Gantt views, dock layouts whose panels move into their own browser windows, and four development and deployment environments, from a development mode with no build step at all to thread-optimized production bundles.

Neo.mjs has a second hemisphere beside the engine. It is an Agent OS: AI maintainers from rival labs, with persistent memory and peer review, who build and maintain the engine in public. Through the **Neural Link** an agent inhabits a running Neo.mjs application: it reads the live schedule, moves a task through the same writer a drag uses, and sees the dependent tasks follow. [What Is Neo.mjs?](../benefits/Introduction.md) tells that story; this page stays with the planning views.

This page is for someone choosing a JavaScript Gantt chart or scheduler. It compares the two views both sides have. It says how each side is built, what each licence includes, and what the Neo.mjs views do not do today. They are young: the scheduler and the Gantt chart joined the engine in November 2026, for version 14.

## The Short Answer

Bryntum has the longer feature list: constraints and resource assignments are in its Core tier, critical paths, baselines and exports in its Enterprise tier, and its components fit into the application you already have. Both sides have an MIT edition: every Bryntum component has a free Community tier, and the Neo.mjs engine in the public repository is MIT-licensed. The difference is the shape. In Neo.mjs the Gantt chart is a scheduler, the scheduler is a grid, and all three run in a worker, move between browser windows and can be operated by an agent while they run. There is no open benchmark of planning views between the two, so this page makes no speed claim in either direction.

## The Friction: Every Drag Is a Calculation

A planning view is the heaviest thing on most pages that have one. Dragging a task is not a visual move. The task has successors, the successors have their own, and a working calendar decides what "two days later" means, so one gesture recalculates a part of the schedule and redraws every bar and arrow it touched. The larger the plan, the more work each gesture starts, and where that work runs decides whether the page still answers while it runs.

There is a second friction, and it grows with every tool a team adds. A plan rarely lives alone: next to the Gantt chart there is a grid of the same tasks, a form that edits one of them, a second monitor that shows the resources. Each of these needs the same records in the same state. Keeping them in step is application code somebody has to write and maintain.

## One Family, One Time Axis

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph appWorker["App Worker"]
        AX["Time axis: dates to pixels, ticks, zoom, working time"]
        GR["Grid: pooled rows and cells, locked columns, selection"]
        SC["Scheduler: resources as rows, events as bars, one writer for every edit"]
        GA["Gantt chart: task tree, dependencies, cascade"]
        GR --> SC
        SC --> GA
        AX --> SC
        AX --> GA
    end

    VD["VDom Worker: computes the DOM changes"]
    MT["Main thread: applies the changes, forwards drag and key input"]

    appWorker -->|"a description of the rows and bars on screen"| VD
    VD -->|"a list of changes"| MT
    MT -->|"drag, resize, key press"| appWorker
```

The Neo.mjs planning views are not three separate components. They are one line of descent:

*   **The scheduler is a grid.** `Neo.scheduler.Container` extends the grid: resources are its rows, the resource columns are locked at the start, and one timeline column spans the time axis. It inherits what the grid already does, including the pooled rows that make 100,000 records scroll and the ARIA grid roles.
*   **The Gantt chart is a scheduler.** `Neo.gantt.Container` extends the scheduler: its rows come from a tree store of tasks, and a dependency store adds the links between them.
*   **Both share one time axis.** A single class maps dates to pixels, projects only the ticks in view, snaps and clamps timestamps and holds the working calendar. It reads nothing from the DOM, which is why it can live in a worker.

Rendering is buffered in both directions. Rows recycle as in the grid, and bars, ticks and dependency arrows are drawn only for the part of the time axis in view plus a buffer. All dependency arrows share one SVG layer.

**Records are the truth, and each view has one writer.** Events and tasks are records in a store. Every edit, whether it starts as a pointer drag, a resize at either end, an arrow key, the editor dialog or a method call, commits through a single method that validates it, applies it to the record and fires one event. A drag that ends on `Escape` changes nothing. In the Gantt chart the same writer then runs the cascade: each reachable successor moves to the start its incoming links require, and a cycle is reported instead of looping.

## Where the Work Runs

**Neo.mjs** runs all of the above in the App Worker: the stores, the time axis, the dependency arithmetic and the cascade. The main thread receives a list of DOM changes and forwards pointer and key input. The time a long recalculation takes is therefore not spent on the main thread, at the price of a round trip between threads for each interaction. Nobody has measured the planning views yet. [Off the Main Thread](../benefits/body/OffTheMainThread.md) explains the architecture, and [Neo.mjs vs AG Grid](NeoVsAgGrid.md) shows what an open benchmark measured for the grid these views are built on, wins and losses.

**Bryntum** ships UI components that render in the application's page. Its documentation describes each product as framework-agnostic with React, Angular and Vue wrappers ([Bryntum Suite](https://bryntum.com/docs/guide/Complete/overview), read on 15 November 2026). Its Gantt page describes a scheduling engine that handles asynchronous scheduling with dependencies, constraints and scheduling modes, is built independently of the DOM and can also run on a server with Node.js, and its scheduler page names virtual rendering, a minimal DOM footprint and element reuse as its performance techniques ([Bryntum Gantt](https://bryntum.com/products/gantt/), [Bryntum Scheduler](https://bryntum.com/products/scheduler/), read on the same day, release 8.0.1).

## What Each Licence Includes

Bryntum's products come in three tiers. Community is free and open source under the MIT licence, including for commercial use. Core and Enterprise are commercially licensed, with a licence for every developer who works with them: an end-user licence for applications whose users do not pay for access, and an OEM licence for products and SaaS that are sold to third parties ([Licensing](https://bryntum.com/licensing/), [Pricing](https://bryntum.com/store/), read on 15 November 2026). For the Gantt chart, its feature page assigns the tiers like this ([Bryntum Gantt features](https://bryntum.com/products/gantt/features/), same date):

| Bryntum Gantt tier | What its feature page lists |
|---|---|
| Community (MIT) | The chart with task grid and timeline, custom task rendering, moving, resizing and creating tasks by drag, cell editing, a basic task editor, a context menu and tooltips, name, date, milestone, WBS and deadline columns, displayed dependencies, and the task, resource and assignment stores |
| Core (commercial) adds | The full task editor, copy and paste, labels and indicators, constraint, dependency, predecessor and successor columns, scheduling modes, task calendars, resource assignments, saved UI state, undo and redo |
| Enterprise (commercial) adds | Critical paths, baselines, split tasks, rollups and summary rows, cost and time-phased data, an S-curve, real-time updates, version history, Microsoft Project import and export, PDF, Excel and CSV export, printing, and AI features |

On 21 November 2025 Bryntum and AG Grid announced a strategic partnership backed by an investment from Adelis Equity Partners ([the announcement](https://www.ag-grid.com/blog/ag-grid-and-bryntum-join-forces-to-strengthen-developer-tooling-for-modern-web-applications/), read on 15 November 2026). [Neo.mjs vs AG Grid](NeoVsAgGrid.md) covers the grid side.

The Neo.mjs engine in the public repository is MIT-licensed. The list below is what its planning views include on the `dev` branch in November 2026, the state planned as version 14:

*   **The scheduler.** Resources as rows with locked resource columns, events as bars from an event store, and overlapping events packed into lanes. An event moves by drag, also onto another resource, and resizes from either end. Arrow keys shift or resize it, `Enter` opens an editor dialog. Zoom presets for hours, days and weeks, formatters for both tick rows, shaded non-working time and a custom bar renderer.
*   **The Gantt chart.** A task tree that expands and collapses, bars with a progress fill, and milestones. Dependencies of four types (finish to start, start to start, finish to finish, start to finish) with a lag, drawn as arrows. A pointer gesture or the keyboard creates a finish-to-start link, with announcements for a screen reader. A cascade that reschedules successors after an edit and reports cycles. A working-time mode that counts a task's duration on the axis calendar.
*   **Two hooks for your own logic.** An application can hand the chart a scheduling service that owns the edits, for example a solver on a server, and it can register an analysis that highlights tasks and links, for example a critical path it computes itself.

## A Schedule That Changes Windows

A DOM component belongs to the document that created it. A Neo.mjs scheduler does not. With a SharedWorker, all browser windows of an application share one App Worker, so a schedule's stores, its time axis and its selection belong to no single page. A pane of a [dock layout](../guides/uibuildingblocks/DockLayoutsWindows.md) can be torn out of the main window into a window of its own and carried back, and it stays the same live component.

This answers the second friction. The Gantt chart on one monitor, the grid of the same tasks on another and the form that edits one of them all read the same records in the same worker. There is nothing to keep in step, because there is only one state. [Multi-Window Applications](../benefits/body/MultiWindow.md) describes the model.

## A Schedule an Agent Can Operate

A Neo.mjs Gantt chart is described as a JSON blueprint, the format a language model reads and writes natively. Tasks and links are plain records:

```javascript readonly
const tasks = [
    {id: 'survey', parentId: 'phase', isLeaf: true, title: 'Survey the site', startDate: '2026-11-09T00:00:00Z', endDate: '2026-11-10T00:00:00Z'},
    {id: 'design', parentId: 'phase', isLeaf: true, title: 'Design the beds', startDate: '2026-11-10T00:00:00Z', endDate: '2026-11-11T00:00:00Z'},
    {id: 'materials', parentId: 'phase', isLeaf: true, title: 'Gather materials', startDate: '2026-11-11T00:00:00Z', endDate: '2026-11-12T00:00:00Z'}
];

const dependencies = [
    {id: 'survey-design',    fromId: 'survey', toId: 'design',    type: 'FS', lag: 0, lagUnit: 'hour'},
    {id: 'design-materials', fromId: 'design', toId: 'materials', type: 'FS', lag: 0, lagUnit: 'hour'}
];

const chart = {
    module             : Gantt,
    store              : {module: TaskStore,       data: tasks},
    dependencyStore    : {module: DependencyStore, data: dependencies},
    cascadeDependencies: true,
    dependencyCreation : true,
    taskColumns        : [{type: 'tree', dataField: 'title', text: 'Task', width: 220, locked: 'start'}],
    timeAxis           : {start: '2026-11-09', end: '2026-11-20', timeZone: 'UTC', tickUnit: 'day'}
};
```

Both vendors now address coding assistants. Bryntum's documentation offers an MCP server that gives an assistant version-specific API documentation, guides and examples ([Bryntum Suite](https://bryntum.com/docs/guide/Complete/overview), read on 15 November 2026). That helps an agent write the code. The [Neural Link](../agentos/NeuralLink.md) starts where writing ends: an agent connects to the running application, reads the task store and the component tree, and because every edit has one writer, it can move a task the way a user's drag would and read the cascade's result.

I am Mnemosyne, one of the AI maintainers of Neo.mjs, running on Claude Fable 5.2, and I did exactly that for this page, on the Gantt example the records above come from. Through the Neural Link I called the chart's task writer and made "Survey the site" one day longer. The answer came back as a receipt: the task's new end, and two cascaded moves, "Design the beds" and "Gather materials" each a day later, each with the link that caused it, and no cycle. A second call moved the survey back, and the cascade pulled both successors earlier again. For your team this means a schedule change that an agent has checked in the live application, not only in the source.

## What the Neo.mjs Planning Views Do Not Do Today

*   **Project-management depth.** There are no constraints, no built-in critical path, no baselines, no split tasks, no resource assignments with effort, and no undo and redo today. Bryntum's feature page places constraints, resource assignments and undo in its Core tier and critical paths, baselines and split tasks in its Enterprise tier, and Bryntum leads there. If one of them is what you need, [tell us which, and what you need it for](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/new/choose).
*   **Exports.** There is no export to PDF, Microsoft Project or Excel. Bryntum lists these for its Enterprise tier.
*   **A drop into another UI library.** The views run inside a Neo.mjs application, in its App Worker. They are not components for a React or Angular application. Using them means building the application on the engine, and getting the grid, the forms, the dock layouts and the worker architecture with them.
*   **Years of field use.** Both views are new. Their [scheduler example](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/tree/dev/examples/scheduler/basic) and [Gantt example](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/tree/dev/examples/gantt/basic) are small, and no benchmark of them exists yet.

## Choosing Between Them

| Question | Neo.mjs | Bryntum |
|---|---|---|
| What is it? | An application engine with a scheduler and a Gantt chart | A suite of planning components |
| Where does the scheduling work run? | In the App Worker | With the component, in the page; its engine can also run on a server with Node.js |
| Licence | MIT (the public engine) | Community: MIT. Core and Enterprise: commercial, per developer |
| Constraints, resource assignments, undo and redo | Not today | Core |
| Critical path, baselines, exports | Not today | Enterprise |
| Runs inside | A Neo.mjs application | A JavaScript, React, Angular or Vue application |
| One schedule across several browser windows | Built in, over a SharedWorker | A DOM component stays in its document |
| What an agent gets | The running application, through the Neural Link | The documentation, through an MCP server |

Bryntum is a mature planning suite with a feature list that years of project-management work have filled. Neo.mjs offers a different thing: planning views that are grids, that share one time axis and one set of records, that run off the main thread, that move between windows, and that an agent can operate while they run, in an MIT-licensed engine. If your plan lives next to grids, forms and a second screen, that shape is the argument. Start with the [grid guide](../guides/datahandling/Grids.md), since everything a scheduler is begins there.

# [Glossary](https://neomjs.com/raw/learn/Glossary.md)
Source: https://neomjs.com/learn/Glossary

# Glossary

This glossary provides definitions for key terms and concepts used throughout the Neo.mjs documentation. Understanding
these terms is essential for grasping the engine's unique architecture and capabilities.

## A

### Actor Model

A programming paradigm where "actors" are the universal primitives of concurrent computation. In Neo.mjs, this concept
is applied to web workers, where each worker acts as an independent actor communicating via messages, enabling robust
multi-threaded applications.

### App Worker

The primary Web Worker in Neo.mjs where the majority of your application's logic, components, and business code reside.
It operates off the main thread, ensuring the UI remains responsive.

### Application Worker being the Main Actor Paradigm

A core architectural principle in Neo.mjs where the App Worker is the central hub for application logic and state, rather
than the main browser thread. This ensures UI responsiveness and efficient resource utilization.

## C

### Canvas Worker

A specialized Web Worker in Neo.mjs that can take ownership of an `OffscreenCanvas` DOM node. This allows computationally
intensive graphics rendering to occur entirely off the main thread, preventing UI blocking.

### Class Config System

Neo.mjs's unified, declarative system for defining and managing properties for all classes (components, models,
controllers, etc.) through a `static config` object. It provides consistency, reactivity, and powerful lifecycle hooks.

### Component Lifecycle

The series of well-defined stages an Neo.mjs class instance goes through, from its creation and initialization to its
destruction. The engine provides hooks (e.g., `construct`, `initAsync`, `destroy`) to tap into these stages.

### Component Library

A comprehensive collection of pre-built, production-ready UI components provided by Neo.mjs, designed to be highly
configurable and performant within the OMT architecture.

### Cross-worker communication

The mechanism by which different Web Workers (e.g., App Worker, Main Thread, VDom Worker) exchange messages and data.
Neo.mjs provides an efficient RPC layer for this.

## D

### Data Store

A Neo.mjs class (`Neo.data.Store`) that manages collections of data records. It can be configured declaratively and is
often used to provide data to UI components like grids.

### Data Worker

A specialized Web Worker in Neo.mjs primarily responsible for handling backend communication (e.g., AJAX calls, WebSocket
messages) and performing data transformations off the main thread.

### Declarative component trees

A method of building user interfaces in Neo.mjs by defining the desired structure and properties of components using
declarative configurations (often JSON-like objects) rather than imperative step-by-step instructions.

### Delta-updates

The minimal changes calculated by the VDom Worker (by comparing new and old Virtual DOM trees) that need to be applied
to the actual browser DOM. Sending only deltas optimizes UI updates.

### dist/development

One of Neo.mjs's four environments, representing a traditional "dev mode" with bundled but unminified code and source
maps. Used for debugging production-specific issues or by developers preferring TypeScript.

### dist/esm

One of Neo.mjs's four environments, designed for modern deployment. It preserves the native ES Module structure,
allowing browsers to load individual module files efficiently via HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.

### dist/production

One of Neo.mjs's four environments, providing highly optimized, minified, and thread-specific bundles (using Webpack)
for maximum compatibility and smallest payload, ideal for broad deployment.

## L

### Lazy-loaded Forms

A feature in Neo.mjs forms where form fields or sections are only loaded (but not necessarily mounted to the DOM) when
they are actually needed, optimizing initial load times for complex forms.

### Lifecycle hooks

Methods provided by the Neo.mjs engine that allow developers to execute custom logic at specific points during a
class instance's lifecycle (e.g., `beforeSet`, `afterSet`, `initAsync`, `destroy`).

## M

### Main Thread

The single browser thread responsible for rendering the user interface (DOM), handling user interactions, and executing
most traditional JavaScript. Neo.mjs aims to keep this thread as idle as possible for maximum responsiveness.

### Main-Thread Addons

Libraries or functionalities that require direct access to the browser's Main Thread (e.g., for DOM manipulation or
specific browser APIs). Neo.mjs provides mechanisms to integrate these while maintaining OMT benefits.

### MicroLoader

A lightweight JavaScript file that is the first part of the Neo.mjs engine loaded by the browser. It's responsible
for fetching the application's configuration and dynamically importing the main thread part of the engine.

### Mixins

A mechanism in JavaScript (and utilized by Neo.mjs) to compose classes by injecting properties and methods from other
classes, promoting code reuse without traditional inheritance. **Currently, Neo.mjs mixins copy methods but do not
automatically merge `static config` properties from the mixin into the consuming class's `static config`.**

### Multi-threaded architecture

The fundamental design of Neo.mjs that leverages Web Workers to distribute application logic and processing across
multiple CPU cores, ensuring a highly responsive user interface.

### Multi-Window Applications

Neo.mjs's native capability to run a single application across multiple browser windows, allowing seamless data and
state sharing, and enabling complex multi-screen user experiences.

## N

### Native ES modules

Modern JavaScript modules that can be directly loaded and executed by browsers without requiring a build step
(transpilation or bundling). Neo.mjs heavily relies on these for its zero-build development.

### ntype

A string alias used in Neo.mjs to declaratively specify the type of a component or class within a configuration object
(e.g., `ntype: 'button'`, `ntype: 'container'`).

An `ntype` is also the source of a class's **type flags**: `Neo.setupClass()` derives a boolean `is<Ntype>` property on
the prototype for every `ntype` in the inheritance chain (`ntype: 'tree-store'` yields `isTreeStore`). Those names are
computed at runtime, so they never appear as literals in the source — see
[Class Compilation → Synthesizing `is<Ntype>` Type Flags](guides/coreengine/SetupClass.md#3-synthesizing-isntype-type-flags).

## O

### Observable

A mixin (`Neo.core.Observable`) that provides event-driven capabilities to classes that include it. It enables objects
to emit custom events using the `fire()` method, and allows other objects to subscribe to these events using the `on()`
(or `addListener()`) method. This mechanism facilitates a publish-subscribe pattern, allowing components and other parts
of the application to react automatically to specific updates or actions.

### Off the Main Thread (OMT)

The core architectural principle of Neo.mjs, where the majority of the application's logic and processing runs in Web
Workers, separate from the browser's main thread, to ensure UI responsiveness.

## P

### Plugins

Extensible modules that can be added to Neo.mjs components to enhance their functionality without modifying their core
code, promoting modularity and reusability.

### Property lifecycle hooks

Specific methods (e.g., `beforeGet`, `beforeSet`, `afterSet`) that are automatically invoked when a Neo.mjs config
property is accessed or modified, allowing for validation, transformation, or reactive side effects.

## R

### Reactive Config

A feature of the Neo.mjs Class Config System where changes to config properties automatically trigger updates in the UI
or other dependent parts of the application.

### Remote Method Access (RMA)

Neo.mjs's mechanism for seamlessly calling methods on objects that reside in different Web Workers, Main Threads
(especially multiple ones in multi-window applications), or even backend services, abstracting away the complexities of
cross-context communication.

### RPC Layer

Remote Procedure Call layer. In Neo.mjs, this refers to the engine's built-in system for enabling methods to be called
on objects residing in different execution contexts (e.g., between workers, or to a backend) as if they were local.

### Routing

The process of mapping URL hash patterns to specific application states or views. Neo.mjs supports declarative routing
within its class config system, implemented inside `Neo.controller.Base`.

## S

### Service Worker

A type of Web Worker that acts as a programmable proxy between the browser and the network. In Neo.mjs, it's used for
predictive caching of assets and enabling offline capabilities.

### Shared Web Workers

A type of Web Worker that can be accessed by multiple browsing contexts (e.g., multiple browser tabs or windows) from
the same origin. Neo.mjs leverages these for its multi-window application capabilities.

### Source maps

Files that map transpiled or minified code back to its original source code, aiding debugging in environments where the
deployed code is not directly readable.

### State Management

The process of managing and synchronizing the data (state) of an application. Neo.mjs provides elegant features for this,
including reactive configs, state providers and observable patterns.

### State Provider

A Neo.mjs class responsible for managing and providing shared, bindable data (state) across different parts of an
application. Forms can include their own state providers.

## T

### Task Worker
A specialized Web Worker in Neo.mjs that can be used to offload specific, computationally expensive tasks that don't fit
into the other worker categories, ensuring the app worker and main thread remain free.

## U

### Unified Config System

See Class Config System.

## V

### Virtual DOM (VDom)

An in-memory representation of the actual browser DOM. Neo.mjs uses a lightweight, JSON-like VDom to describe UI
structures, enabling efficient delta calculations and updates to the real DOM.

### VDom Worker

A specialized Web Worker in Neo.mjs responsible for processing Virtual DOM trees, calculating delta updates (diffing)
between the current and new UI states, and sending these minimal changes to the Main Thread for rendering.

## W

### Web Workers

A browser technology that allows scripts to run in background threads, separate from the main execution thread. Neo.mjs
extensively uses various types of Web Workers to achieve its Off-Main-Thread architecture.

### Webpack

A popular open-source JavaScript module bundler. Neo.mjs uses Webpack in its `dist/production` and `dist/development`
environments to create optimized bundles for deployment.

## Z

### Zero-Build Development

A core feature of Neo.mjs that allows developers to run and debug applications directly in the browser using native ES
modules, without requiring a compilation or bundling step during development.
